story: This is a landscape of contrasts packed into one corner of Spitsbergen. In the west, old metamorphic rock has been cut by ice into sharp alpine peaks and narrow sounds; in the east, red Devonian sandstone builds massive mountains. Between them, at Bockfjorden, the cone of Sverrefjellet is the remains of a volcano, and warm springs rise near the shore, building terraces of carbonate. They are among the northernmost hot springs known on land anywhere. To the north-east lies Reinsdyrflya, the largest strandflat in Svalbard.

The last of the Atlantic's warm water, carried north by the West Spitsbergen Current, keeps the west-coast fjords largely free of ice for much of the year. Seabirds crowd the cliffs, eiders and geese nest on the islets, and walruses haul out on Moffen. Svalbard reindeer and Arctic foxes live on the tundra, and polar bears den here, hunting ringed seals and raiding the islets for eggs. Around the springs at Bockfjorden grow plants found nowhere else in Svalbard.

Europeans came for whales. English whalers set up a station at Gravneset in Magdalenefjorden after 1614, and the Dutch built Smeerenburg, "blubber town", on Amsterdamøya around 1620, with as many as 200 men ashore in summer boiling blubber into oil. When the bowhead whales close to shore were gone and whaling moved out to sea, the stations were left; around 1660 Smeerenburg was abandoned. The graves of those who died, about 130 at Gravneset and 165 on Ytre Norskøya, are among the largest burial grounds in Svalbard.

In the 1890s the corner became a launch pad for the North Pole. Salomon August Andrée built a balloon hangar at Virgohamna in 1896 and took off from it in July 1897, never to return; the American Walter Wellman tried three times by airship from the same bay between 1906 and 1909. The national park was created on 1 June 1973. It now holds the busiest tourist landings in Svalbard outside the settlements, and since 2025 tourist landings have been confined to designated sites, except on frozen ground in winter and spring.
howItWorks: Svalbard has its own law, the Svalbard Environmental Protection Act. The public right of access applies here too, but no travel may damage, litter or needlessly disturb people or wildlife. Polar bears may not be disturbed, attracted or pursued, and no one may come closer to a bear than 300 metres, or 500 metres from 1 March to 30 June; anyone who finds a bear inside that distance must withdraw. Everyone outside the settlements, except people on an organised tour, must know how to guard against a polar bear attack and carry the means to scare one off. Every trace of people from before 1946 is a protected monument with a 100-metre zone around it, where you may not pitch a tent or light a fire without permission (a tent on frozen, snow-covered ground is the exception). From 1 April to 31 August no ship's horn, shot or other loud noise is allowed within a nautical mile of a bird cliff, and no drone within 500 metres of one.

The field-safety regulation (feltsikkerhetsforskriften, FOR-2025-06-06-940), in force since 1 January 2026, decides who must tell the Governor of Svalbard (Sysselmesteren) before setting out. The whole park lies outside the 'travel area' (ferdselsområde, the former management area 10) around central Spitsbergen. An independent visitor must notify the Governor at least four weeks ahead and wait for the reply, carry equipment to raise the alarm and talk both ways, and hold insurance or a guarantee for search and rescue, with a ceiling of NOK 120,000 to 650,000 per operation depending on the zone. Residents of Svalbard must notify the Governor before travelling in this park too. Tour operators need the Governor's permission; a requirement for them to use approved Svalbard guides has been adopted, but its start date has yet to be set.

The park's own regulation bans off-road vehicles, snowmobiles included, and aircraft landings, and forbids flying lower than 300 metres within a nautical mile of land. Drones are banned, and ships with more than 200 passengers may not enter the park's waters. Tourist landings are allowed only on frozen, snow-covered ground from 1 January to 25 May, or at designated landing sites, always with a guide. Marked areas around the whaling remains at Ytre Norskøya, Likneset and Ebeltofthamna, and the area round the Troll springs (Trollkjeldene), are closed all year. The bird reserves inside the park, among them Moseøya, Skorpa and Guissezholmen, are closed to all traffic from 15 May to 15 August, and the Moffen reserve from 15 May to 15 September.

sightNotes.poi-no-nordvest-spitsbergen-gravneset-ma: A whalers' cemetery of about 130 graves from the 1600s to the late 1700s and four blubber ovens, below glaciers. Keep outside the fences.
sightNotes.poi-no-nordvest-spitsbergen-smeerenburg: The main Dutch whaling station of the early 1600s, on Amsterdamøya. Rings of 'blubber cement' mark the ovens; do not step on them.
sightNotes.poi-no-nordvest-spitsbergen-virgohamna: The bay on Danskøya where Andrée launched his polar balloon in 1897 and Wellman based his airships. Protected remains; check the Governor's access rules.
sightNotes.poi-no-nordvest-spitsbergen-ytre-norskoy: Nine Dutch blubber ovens along a beach and one of Svalbard's largest burial grounds, 165 graves. Parts of the site are closed all year.
sightNotes.poi-no-nordvest-spitsbergen-jotunkjelden: Warm springs near the shore, at 20 °C or more all year, building fragile carbonate terraces. Walk on the moraine, never on the deposits.
sightNotes.poi-no-nordvest-spitsbergen-monacobreen: One of the park's two great glaciers, calving into the head of Liefdefjorden. Keep well back from the ice front.
sightNotes.poi-no-nordvest-spitsbergen-reinsdyrflya: The largest strandflat in Svalbard: a low plain of old beaches and tundra between the open sea and Woodfjorden.
sightNotes.poi-no-nordvest-spitsbergen-moffen: A low gravel island just north of 80° North and a walrus haul-out. All traffic, by sea or air below 500 metres, is banned from 15 May to 15 September.

entrances: By sea from Longyearbyen up the west coast, on an expedition cruise or a smaller boat
There are no roads, and snowmobiles and other off-road vehicles may not enter the park
planYourVisit.reservations: There is no entry permit, but an independent visitor must notify the Governor of Svalbard at least four weeks before the trip and wait for the reply. Most visitors come with a tour operator, as the national park service recommends; the operator holds the Governor's permission and takes care of the formalities.
permits: Notification to the Governor four weeks ahead, with insurance or a guarantee for search and rescue
Tourist landings only at designated landing sites, or on frozen, snow-covered ground from 1 January to 25 May, and always with a guide
Camping in the same place for a week or more needs the Governor's permission
A rifle for polar bear protection can be hired only with a firearms licence, a European Firearms Pass or the Governor's permission — check the current rules
camping: Wild camping is allowed under the right of access, outside the 100-metre zone around protected monuments (a tent on frozen, snow-covered ground excepted)
Keep the means to scare off a polar bear at hand in every camp
lodging: None in the park; Longyearbyen is the base for almost every trip
seasonalClosures: The bird reserves inside the park are closed to all traffic from 15 May to 15 August
Moffen nature reserve is closed to all traffic, including boats and low flights, from 15 May to 15 September
Outside the designated sites, tourist landings are allowed only on frozen, snow-covered ground from 1 January to 25 May
Rules change: check the Governor of Svalbard's current regulations before you go

chronology.text: English whalers enter Magdalenefjorden and later set up a station at Gravneset.
The Dutch build Smeerenburg on Amsterdamøya, their main whaling station.
With the inshore whales gone, Smeerenburg is abandoned.
Salomon August Andrée builds a balloon hangar at Virgohamna.
Andrée's balloon lifts off from Virgohamna for the North Pole; the expedition is lost.
Walter Wellman makes three attempts on the Pole by airship from Virgohamna.
Nordvest-Spitsbergen National Park is established on 1 June.
Tour operators must follow site-specific guidelines at busy sites such as Smeerenburg and Ytre Norskøya, and the Trollkjeldene springs are closed to traffic.
Tourist landings are limited to designated sites and frozen ground, drones are banned and ships with more than 200 passengers barred from the park's waters.
The field-safety regulation takes effect: independent visitors must notify the Governor four weeks ahead.

safety: Polar bears can appear anywhere, at any time of year. Keep a constant lookout, carry the means to scare a bear off, and know how to use them; the Governor recommends a rifle as the primary protection.
Help is far away. Carry equipment to raise the alarm and talk both ways — outside the travel area the law requires it — and leave your plan with someone who will act on it.
Glacier fronts calve without warning and send waves across the fjord. Keep well back from ice cliffs, on land and in a boat.
Walruses are protected and can be dangerous in the water. Keep your distance, and check that no walruses are on a beach before choosing where to land.
regulations: Keep at least 300 metres from polar bears, and 500 metres from 1 March to 30 June.
Snowmobiles and other off-road vehicles, aircraft landings and drones are banned in the park.
Ships with more than 200 passengers may not enter the park's waters; tourist landings only at designated sites or on frozen, snow-covered ground from 1 January to 25 May, with a guide.
Everything left by people before 1946 is a protected monument: do not touch, move or take it, and keep outside fenced graves and ovens.
Plants and fossils may not be removed.

fees.detail: Paid by every visitor to Svalbard except residents: collected with the ticket for the flight out of Svalbard, or by the travel organiser. It goes to the Svalbard Environmental Protection Fund.

weather: The climate is Arctic, eased on the west coast by the warm current that keeps the fjords largely open. Summer is cool and often foggy, and snow can fall in any month; wind can rise quickly on open water. In Longyearbyen the midnight sun lasts from about 20 April to late August and the polar night from late October to mid-February, and this far north the sun stays up longer still. Most visitors come by ship in summer, when the fjords are open.
directions: Fly to Svalbard Airport, Longyear, which has scheduled flights from Oslo and Tromsø. No roads link the settlements, and off-road vehicles may not enter the park, so the way in is by sea: expedition ships and smaller boats sail north from Longyearbyen along the west coast to Magdalenefjorden, Smeerenburgfjorden and Woodfjorden. Ny-Ålesund, the research settlement on Kongsfjorden, is the nearest settlement to the park's southern edge. Ships with more than 200 passengers may not enter the park's waters.
